title: Private Equity Is Cashing in on Autism Therapy. Children Are Paying the Price aying-the-price/
author: Beth Hawkins
summary: Beth Hawkins and Nicholas Perez use the 275 million record Medicaid billing dataset released by DOGE to reconstruct six years of spending on applied behavior analysis, the dominant autism therapy, and find that roughly $7 billion flowed to providers while private equity firms consolidated the field. Their central argument is not simply that fraud exists but that the regulatory design invited extraction: public money was turned on before oversight was built, and ABA industry standards prescribe the same high intensity of treatment for every child regardless of age or need. The education stakes are the point of the piece. Because Medicaid rules forbid academic instruction inside standalone therapy centers, federal audits in Colorado, Indiana, Wisconsin and Maine found school-age children spending years in full-time therapy instead of classrooms, with providers warning parents that enrolling a child in kindergarten would cause regression. The reporters trace the history from Ole Ivar Lovaas through Lorri Unumb's 2005 insurance mandate campaign and the 2014 Affordable Care Act clarification, and they document how twenty-three of the fifty largest billers came under private equity ownership. Woven through is the evidence that ABA itself is contested, including research linking participation to higher rates of mental health hospitalization and PTSD symptoms. The piece ends on an opportunity cost, arguing the same $2 billion a year could staff every district in the country with occupational therapists who have demonstrated results.
points: Medicaid claims across the six most common autism therapy billing codes rose 381 percent between 2019 and 2024, from roughly $400 million a year to nearly $2 billion, with private equity backed providers billing the most.

Because Medicaid law bars therapists in standalone ABA centers from teaching academics, federal audits found school-age children parked in therapy for years, including one Colorado child who stayed until age 16 at a total cost of $518,700.
Twenty-three of the fifty largest ABA billers are private equity owned, a structure the reporters argue rewards short-term extraction and insulates investors from liability for fraud or harm.

The reporting traces the industry's legal foundation to Lorri Unumb's 2005 insurance mandate campaign in South Carolina and the 2014 clarification that the Affordable Care Act obliged Medicaid to fund autism treatment.

Hawkins and Perez close with an opportunity cost: redirecting the $2 billion spent annually on ABA into school budgets could put one full-time and one half-time occupational therapist in every district in the country.
quotes: And it shows how a well-intentioned campaign by parents desperate to find a “cure” for their autistic kids has mushroomed into a poorly implemented but extremely lucrative mechanism for providing ABA — a system of rewards and punishments designed to eliminate certain behaviors — to as many autistic children as possible, regardless of their age or actual needs.

Pediatricians, psychologists and other professionals who diagnose autism reflexively prescribe ABA to parents, typically unaware that there is mounting disagreement about the therapy’s effectiveness and the associated trauma that can follow an autistic individual into adulthood.

From 2019 to 2024, The 74 found, Medicaid claims for the six most common autism therapy billing codes shot up some 381%, from $400 million a year to nearly $2 billion — with private equity-backed providers leading the billing pack.

The four federal audits of state Medicaid spending released so far show what advocates have long decried: ABA service providers are allowed to keep children in lucrative standalone treatment centers where they are barred by Medicaid law from receiving academic instruction — often for years after they should begin attending school.

The audit found one Colorado child, referred for ABA in 2009 at the age of 2, who continued receiving six or more hours of treatment five days a week until age 16 — without any independent evaluation that ABA treatment was still appropriate.

Special education teachers say that when these students show up in a classroom, it’s after years of lost academic instruction. In practice, often this means they will be denied the chance to learn alongside their typically developing peers — a right enshrined in federal law.

Private equity typically acquires privately held companies that have access to steady streams of revenue, extracting as much cash as possible in the short term and leaving debt when investors move on.

[Private equity firms] have nothing to lose if something goes bankrupt,” says Rosemary Batt, one of the authors of the Center for Economic and Policy Research report and a professor emeritus at the Industrial and Labor Relations School at Cornell University. “If a company gets caught in fraud, it’s just the cost of doing business.
